body.text: Weak institutional foundations, hidden lifecycle costs, and fragmented coordination risk turning PM-eBus Sewa into a fleet-building exercise rather than a public transport reform

Approved in 2023, India’s ambitious PM-eBus Sewa programme aims to deploy 10,000 air-conditioned electric buses (e-buses) across 115 cities in 20 states and 6 union territories. An allocation of INR 576.130 billion supports this effort, with 4,330 buses contracted in 53 cities and services already operational in Guwahati, Bhavnagar, Nagpur, and Chandigarh.

However, these numbers don’t inspire confidence when read against India’s existing bus deficit. A recent Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) study shows that of the 14.5 lakh registered buses across the country, about 65,000 operate as organised urban buses. This provides 13.3-13.8 buses per lakh of urban population, 70 percent less than the government norm of 44 buses per lakh citizens. More than 400 cities have no organised bus service. Other research also shows that most Indian cities do not meet the per-lakh-population standard set by the Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs (MoHUA).
The 10,000 e-buses under PM-eBus Sewa will only cover a small part of this gap. The real question, therefore, is whether India is creating a fleet without building a better public transport system.

Under the PM-eBus Sewa scheme, the Gross Cost Contract model allows Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) or leasing firms to provide and operate buses for a per-kilometre fee based on distance travelled. At the same time, the authority receives the fare revenue. The adoption of this model has allowed companies like Convergence Energy Services Limited (CESL) to pool orders, create larger volumes, and benefit from lower prices. However, the perennial losses suffered by operational State Transport Undertakings (STUs) raise a challenge.

According to the Institute of Energy Economic and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) data puts the total STU debt at about INR 380 billion (US$4.6 billion). STUs also have a history of defaulting on payments to fuel suppliers, other contractors, and employees. It is this payment risk, and not battery technology, that causes the OEMs not to participate: an INR 50 billion tender floated by CESL received no quotes from any manufacturers, and several cities like Kochi, Lucknow, and Bhopal faced several failed tenders, with Kochi only receiving one bid in the first two rounds. Although the government’s Payment Security Mechanism with a budget of INR 34.35 billion seeks to mitigate defaults, it does nothing to alleviate the STUs’ weak performance. Thus, a risk allocation process laid on paper does not automatically allocate it to whoever can actually manage it.

Ongoing discussions about cost focus on upfront procurement cost, but the more important costs come later. In the Indian e-bus market, a battery pack of about 250–320 kWh costs between INR 3 and 4.5 million and lasts approximately 7 to 8 years. At the same time, the warranty period is only 5 to 6 years. This implies that battery pack degradation will lead to costs for STUs that manufacturers do not cover, occurring when STUs are least able to absorb unexpected capital expenditure.
The whole-life-cost accounting method needs to be integrated into the procurement process so it is not an afterthought during contract implementation.

Moreover, because GCC contracts usually outlive battery warranty periods, current tender processes leave a gap in the fiscal costing mechanism. The whole-life-cost accounting method needs to be integrated into the procurement process so it is not an afterthought during contract implementation.
The shift from diesel and CNG to electric buses requires a workforce that can drive, maintain, and repair battery-powered vehicles, yet India has not built the skilling pipeline to produce one.

A National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) study conducted in 2025 showed a demand-supply mismatch, which slows the process, along with a lack of qualified trainers and battery-technology courses. Some companies are already leading the workforce transition. For instance, NueGo claims it has trained over 3,000 drivers for its e-buses, but the process is led by individual organisations rather than being systematic.

Moreover, different route characteristics lead to widely varying battery sizes, charging schedules, and vehicle specification requirements, including route distance, incline, passenger load, traffic, and weather. Therefore, using standardised procurement categories can result in excessive battery size on short routes and insufficient battery size on longer or higher-demand routes, leading to high capital costs in the first case and possible breakdowns in the second case. A route-oriented approach that lays out operational requirements before selecting vehicles would optimise battery size and make the process more efficient.

Additionally, bus services involve state transport undertakings, municipal authorities, state transport agencies, private operators, electricity distribution companies (DISCOMs), and banks and manufacturers, each with different objectives, without a single authority overseeing the efficiency of the whole process. This scenario usually results in achieving procurement goals without improving service efficiency and customer satisfaction.

Realising the potential of vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology requires transport authorities and DISCOMs to plan jointly, fostering a partnership essential for effective system integration and progress.

E-bus depots create a new and considerable electricity market, with about 100 e-buses requiring 4-5 MW of electricity. At the same time, some larger depots can utilise as much as 60-70 MW of power, which can strain the already outdated distribution system and force them to charge at higher electricity prices. Realising the potential of vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology requires transport authorities and DISCOMs to plan jointly, fostering a partnership essential for effective system integration and progress.

While electrification must happen, procurement goals should not be treated as a metric for transformation. The next step should be to establish a performance framework based on reliability, travel frequency, reach, affordability, and accessibility. The transition strategy should also include contract design, lifecycle costing, personnel training, route design, and sector coordination.
The number of e-buses deployed must not be used to evaluate the success of India’s e-bus programme, but rather by whether the system serves citizens better than their cars will ten years from now.
